state.case_summary:
A 37-year-old woman presented with 6 hours of acute hypogastric pain and nausea. She reported occasional postprandial abdominal discomfort but had no history of abdominal surgery, trauma, or chronic illness. On examination, there was localized tenderness in the right lower abdomen and hypogastrium with a positive McBurney’s sign and rebound tenderness; bowel sounds were normal and there was no distention. Laboratory studies showed a white-cell count of 19,000/μL; other values were unremarkable. Initial differential diagnoses included acute appendicitis, gynecological disorders, and inflammatory bowel disease. An abdominal radiograph and pelvic ultrasonography were negative for gynecological pathology and were inconclusive for appendicitis. A contrast-enhanced CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis (axial, coronal, and sagittal reformats) demonstrated an abnormally low transverse colon and right colic flexure, with small-bowel loops clustered above and to the right. The third portion of the duodenum was not seen in its expected location. There was an abnormal superior mesenteric artery–vein relationship, with the vein coursing to the left of the artery. The clustered loops showed mesenteric congestion with prominent vessels but no signs of ischemia. The appendix appeared normal.
